newsitem.title: UK: IRA upsurge freezes police force cuts plan - media.
newsitem.headline: IRA upsurge freezes police force cuts plan - media.

text.p: An upsurge in IRA violence has forced Northern Ireland's police chief to freeze plans for big job cuts and other major structural changes in his Royal Ulster Constabulary, British media said on Sunday.
A police spokesman refused to divulge details of a review of the force's structures but said staff "are being updated" about its key findings.

The reports came after a mortar attack on a village police station in the British-ruled province, which security sources were convinced was the latest in an escalating campaign by Irish Republican Army guerrillas fighting British rule.

One missile crashed through the roof of the unoccupied base at Tempo in County Fermanagh on Saturday night and the other landed in the station yard. They were fired from a van that burst into flames minutes later.
"Both failed to explode and were defused by army experts," a Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) spokesman said.

Security sources said the missiles were "Mark 15" mortars, known as "barrack-busters", often lethal devices which the IRA has often launched from trucks in a war that was resumed last February after a 17-month ceasefire.
Police said no one was hurt but the attackers put civilian lives at risk. A man and his child drove past the van as the mortars were launched, a spokesman said.
No group claimed the attack but the IRA has admitted other recent incidents which have strained a two-year truce by their pro-British Loyalist foes.

The London Sunday Times said police chief Ronnie Flanagan would formally acknowledge later this week that plans for reform of the largely Protestant 13,500-strong police force had been shelved indefinitely because of escalating violence.
A BBC radio news report said many reforms in a special review of the force, involving the loss of thousands of jobs, had been ruled out some time ago.
The Sunday Times said Flanagan was gloomy about the immediate security situation, having been warned by the RUC Special Branch to expect attacks on VIPs and public buildings.
The reforms, reflecting a reduced need for police counter-insurgency, were widely seen as part of a ceasefire "peace dividend" which evaporated when the guerrillas went back to war.

On the eve of multi-party peace talks in Belfast, Irish Prime Minister Dick Spring warned that IRA attacks were making the conflict more intractable and risked reprisals by pro-British Loyalist militants.
Spring, interviewed in Dublin's Sunday Business Post newspaper, said violence was delaying the prospect of the IRA's Sinn Fein wing getting into the all-party talks.

"My genuine belief is that if there is serious bombing and killing in Northern Ireland or the United Kingdom, you are putting off the chance of getting around the table for a long time. You are also tempting fate about a loyalist response."

Monday's talks, in an eight-month-old process chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, involve all the major parties except the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm which is excluded because the guerrillas refuse to abandon violence.
